ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The given image shows a blank 4×4 grid, with a total of 4 rows and 4 columns, and cells are adjacent by shared edges; diagonal contact does not count as a shared edge. Reasoning: Regard the uncolored cells as cells that must “serve” or touch all the colored cells. The problem requires that every colored cell share an edge with at least one uncolored cell, and at the same time every uncolored cell also share an edge with at least one colored cell. If Ellen colored 13 cells, then only 3 uncolored cells would remain. A cell in a 4×4 grid has at most only 4 shared-edge neighboring cells, so 3 uncolored cells can provide at most 3×4=12 edge-adjacency relationships with colored cells. But each of the 13 colored cells needs at least one such adjacency relationship, so at least 13 adjacency relationships are needed, a contradiction. Therefore it is impossible to color 13 cells, and at most only 12 cells can be colored. Now show that 12 can be done: Let the 4 uncolored cells be located at (row,column)=(1,2), (2,4), (3,1), (4,3), and color all the remaining 12 cells. Checking shows that every colored cell shares an edge with at least one of these 4 uncolored cells; at the same time, beside every uncolored cell there are also colored cells. Therefore 12 colored cells can be achieved, and from the upper bound it is known that this is the maximum value.

method.method_draft: Treat the uncoloured cells as the cells that must 'serve' or touch all coloured cells. From the image, read the grid as a 4 by 4 array with side-adjacency only. From the text, use the condition that every coloured cell must share a side with at least one uncoloured cell. If Ellen coloured 13 cells, then only 3 cells would be uncoloured. But any one cell in a 4 by 4 grid has at most 4 side-neighbours, so 3 uncoloured cells can be adjacent to at most 12 coloured cells in total, even before accounting for overlaps or boundary cells. Thus 13 coloured cells is impossible, so at least 4 cells must be uncoloured and at most 12 can be coloured. Then give an explicit arrangement with 4 uncoloured cells, for example at positions (row,column) (1,2), (2,4), (3,1), and (4,3). Check from the grid that every remaining coloured cell touches one of these uncoloured cells, and each uncoloured cell also touches a coloured cell. Therefore 12 is achievable and maximal.

method.method_draft: Divide the 4 by 4 grid into the four disjoint 2 by 2 corner blocks: top-left, top-right, bottom-left, and bottom-right. From the image, note that each actual corner cell of the whole grid has its only two side-neighbours inside its corresponding 2 by 2 corner block. From the text, every coloured cell must have an uncoloured side-neighbour. Therefore, in each 2 by 2 corner block, at least one cell must be uncoloured; otherwise the corner cell in that block would be coloured and both of its side-neighbours would also be coloured, violating the condition. Since the four 2 by 2 blocks are disjoint, there must be at least 4 uncoloured cells, so at most 16 - 4 = 12 cells can be coloured. To show 12 is possible, leave uncoloured cells at (1,2), (2,4), (3,1), and (4,3), one in each corner block, and colour all other cells. A direct side-neighbour check verifies that every coloured cell touches one of these uncoloured cells and every uncoloured cell touches a coloured cell. Hence the maximum is 12.

所以最大可涂色格数是 12。
